small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of multiples to find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers. Encourage a systematic approach when listing multiples, and discuss with students that, while multiples are infinite, they only need to list enough to identify a common one. Prompt them to highlight any common multiples before identifying the lowest common multiple. Once confident, students can progress to word problems and examples involving more than two numbers. Discuss the difference between the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple, helping students to understand when each one is used. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple. • Students may assume that the product of the two numbers is the lowest common multiple, for example that 36 is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 12 • Students may incorrectly list the multiples of two numbers. small_step_desc: In this extend step, students develop flexibility in representing numbers by expressing them as a product of factors to simplify calculations. Encourage students to rewrite numbers in ways that make mental or written methods more efficient. For example, in the calculation 16 × 50, students could express 16 as 4 × 4 and 50 as 25 × 2, recognising that 4 × 25 = 100 and so simplifying the calculation to 100 × 4 × 2. Discuss the commutative property of multiplication, showing how reordering factors can make calculations easier. The focus is not on prime factorisation but on selecting factor groupings that simplify the process, helping students to develop efficient strategies for working without a calculator. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write a value as a product of its prime factors, without considering how other representations may be more efficient. • Students may attempt to calculate the products in the order they are given, rather than looking for useful factor pairs that simplify the calculation, such as numbers that multiply to make 10 or 100 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 2 – Properties of numbers | Step 11 Mathematical talk • What are some useful factors of a number to identify? • Why is it useful to identify pairs of factors that multiply to give 10 or 100? • Write as a product of its factors. • Is writing a value as a product of its prime factors always the most efficient method? small_step: Draw and measure lines and angles
small_step_name: Draw and measure lines and angles
small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop the practical skills of drawing and measuring line segments and angles accurately, building on understanding from Key Stage 2 Recap the correct use of a ruler for drawing and measuring line segments before introducing the protractor as the tool for measuring and drawing angles. Ensure that students know how to align the baseline and select the correct scale, modelling these skills clearly. Emphasise that an angle is a measure of turn. Provide questions where students both draw given angles and measure angles already drawn. Encourage them to estimate before measuring in order to develop a sense of size. Everyday contexts, such as design or navigation, help to show why accuracy matters. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misalign the protractor baseline with the line segment, leading to inaccurate measurements. • The term “line segment” may be unfamiliar and students may not realise that a line is infinite in length. • Students may read from the wrong scale on the protractor, for example 140° instead of 40°. • Students may misalign the ruler by not positioning the beginning of a line segment at zero. small_step_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and extend their Key Stage 2 understanding of parallel and perpendicular lines. Remind students that parallel lines are always the same distance apart and never meet, no matter how far they are extended. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle (90°), which can be shown using a square corner or set square. Use clear diagrams and practical examples, such as train tracks for parallel lines or the corner of a book for perpendicular lines. Encourage students to spot these relationships in shapes, coordinate grids and the classroom environment. Emphasise accurate vocabulary, such as “intersect” and “right angle”, and correct notation, including arrows for parallel lines and squares for right angles. Students should practise drawing parallel and perpendicular lines using a ruler and protractor or set square. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that all lines that do not meet are parallel, overlooking the fact that parallel lines must also be equidistant. • Students may assume that lines need to be the same length to be parallel. • Students may confuse perpendicular lines with any intersecting lines. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 10 Mathematical talk • How can you tell that two lines are parallel? • What does it mean for two lines to be the same distance apart? • Can parallel lines ever meet? small_step_desc: In this extend step, students are introduced to the sum of the interior angles in a polygon. Start with triangles, where the angles sum to 180°, and quadrilaterals, which can be split into two triangles to give 360°. Explore polygons with more sides by partitioning them into triangles from a single vertex, for example splitting a pentagon into three triangles, making the sum of the interior angles 540°. Encourage students to investigate different polygons and record their findings, noticing how the number of sides links to the number of triangles and the total angle sum. Then introduce regular polygons, showing how each interior angle can be found by dividing the total by the number of sides. Students also identify interior and exterior angles at a vertex and calculate them using their knowledge of angles on a straight line. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that the sum of the interior angles differs between regular and irregular polygons. • Students may assume that the sum of the angles can be found by multiplying the number of sides by 180°. • Students may struggle to split the polygons into triangles, using more than one vertex. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 4 – Angles and polygons | Step 12 Mathematical talk • How many triangles can a quadrilateral be split into? What does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • If a pentagon can be split into three triangles, what does that tell you about the total sum of its interior angles? • Why is the interior angle sum of any polygon always a multiple of 180°? • Describe the relationship between the number of sides a polygon has and the number of triangles it can be split into from one vertex. • How can you calculate the angle sum of any polygon? small_step_desc: In this small step, students identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. Start with several right-angled triangles and ask students to measure the length of each side. Encourage them to identify the side that is opposite the right angle and ask what they notice about its length compared to the other sides. Introduce the term “hypotenuse” and emphasise that this is always the longest side in a right-angled triangle and is always opposite the right angle. Include plenty of examples in different orientations, so that they do not rely on position or direction. Include non-examples to challenge misconceptions. As students develop confidence, ask them to identify the hypotenuses within a compound shape made up of right-angled triangles.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore independent events. Draw students’ attention to how this method produces the same result as multiplying the separate probabilities, for example 1 2 × 1 6 = 1 12 for rolling an even number on one dice and a 5 on the other. Making this connection explains why multiplication is used for independent events and helps to link different approaches. Encourage students to express probabilities as both fractions and decimals, supporting fluency and making comparisons easier. Using diagrams provides opportunities for students to develop accurate reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that “independent” means that the probabilities are equal, rather than that one outcome does not affect the other. • Students may confuse independent with mutually exclusive events, not recognising that mutually exclusive outcomes cannot happen together. small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore probabilities using Venn diagrams. Recap the regions of a Venn diagram, clarifying how each represents a distinct group within the data. Draw students’ attention to how probabilities are calculated, by comparing the number of outcomes in a region with the total represented by the diagram. If appropriate, students could explore the “given that” clause, finding the probability of one event when another is already known to have occurred. This introduces conditional probability in a structured way and highlights how Venn diagrams make relationships between events visual. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may omit elements written outside the circles. • Students may forget to include the intersection when calculating the probability of “A or B”. • Students may think that the total in the denominator should be the sum of the two circles, rather than the overall total. • When answering “given that” questions, students may use the total population instead of restricting it to the given condition. small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding from Year 8, completing and describing reflections in horizontal, vertical and diagonal lines. Some students may not yet have encountered reflections in lines expressed algebraically, or fully described reflections, as these are covered in extend steps in Year 8 Recap how to identify equations of vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines, as this underpins both drawing and describing reflections. Emphasise that a full description must include both the fact that it is a reflection and the equation of the mirror line. As with previous transformations, tracing paper is a useful tool. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not use the perpendicular distance between vertices and a diagonal mirror line. • Students may draw an incorrect reflection when a shape crosses one of the axes. • Students may incorrectly plot lines of the form y = a and x = b, resulting in an incorrect reflection. • Students may use non-mathematical vocabulary to describe a reflection, such as “flip” or “mirror”, rather than “reflect”. small_step_name: Angles around a point, on a straight line and vertically opposite
small_step_desc: In this small step, students revisit key angle facts from Key Stage 3, including angles around a point, angles on a straight line and vertically opposite angles. Begin by recapping these rules using clear diagrams, and asking reasoning questions such as “What is the same and what is different?”, to help students recognise when angles sum to 180° or 360°, and when angles are equal. Emphasise the importance of selecting the correct rule for each scenario, and provide examples that require more than one rule to be applied. Encourage the consistent use of three-letter notation for angles, and correct use of angle symbols throughout. Ask students to explain their reasoning when identifying relationships between angles. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the rules for angles on a straight line and angles around a point, leading to incorrect totals. • Students may not label angles using three-letter notation, or use the wrong notation when justifying their answers. • Students may believe that vertically opposite angles sum to 180° or 360°. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of interior angles of polygons from Key Stage 3. Begin by revisiting the relationship between interior and exterior angles. Highlight that they form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Remind students that the sum of interior angles can be calculated using (n – 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides, and that this can also be used to work out the number of sides when the sum of interior angles is known. It can be useful to model splitting polygons into triangles to demonstrate why this method works to calculate the sum of interior angles. Reinforce that “regular” means that all sides and angles are equal. Calculators may be used throughout this step, so the focus remains on the method rather than the arithmetic. small_step_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their learning of alternate and corresponding angles, as well as introducing co-interior angles. Begin by reviewing the key angle relationships and discuss what is the same and what is different about co-interior angles compared to alternate and corresponding angles. Emphasise that co-interior angles sum to 180° while alternate and corresponding angles are equal. Reinforce that alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles are only formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines. Students should be encouraged to highlight angle pairs, clearly reasoning and justifying their answers. Challenge students further to strengthen reasoning and fluency, by using diagrams that include algebraic expressions and less-familiar orientations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that co-interior angles are equal in size. • Students may assume angles are alternate/corresponding/ co-interior when the lines are not parallel. • Students may not justify their answers even when asked to give reasons for their answers. small_step: Solve problems with angles and algebra
small_step_name: Solve problems with angles and algebra
small_step_desc: In this small step, students apply angle facts and algebraic techniques to solve multi-step geometric problems involving algebraic expressions. Begin by revisiting the key angle relationships, such as angles in polygons and in parallel lines, ensuring that students can justify each fact before using it. Demonstrate how to form and solve equations based on angle facts, and model how to check that solutions are accurate and realistic. Ensure that students build clear chains of reasoning and explain why each step is valid. To strengthen understanding, use problems that involve several intersecting lines, shapes in less familiar orientations and simultaneous angle relationships. Challenge students further by asking them to create and solve their own algebraic angle problems. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may form incorrect equations if they misidentify an angle fact. • Students may assume diagrams are drawn to scale when they are not. • Students may incorrectly simplify algebraic expressions. How can we form an equation based on this? • Can we form any equations? Why or why not? How can this help us to form an equation? • Two co-interior angles are labelled 3x + 22 and x + 55 What do you know about the angles? How can this help us to form an equation? • The interior angles in a pentagon are x, 2x, 3x, 4x and 5x. What angle fact do you know that will help us to form an equation? small_step_desc: In this extend step, students begin to use clear reasoning to prove geometric facts. Start by revisiting familiar angle facts, ensuring students can state each fact accurately. Model how to build a simple chain of reasoning using statements such as “because alternate angles are equal” or “because angles in a triangle sum to 180°”. Encourage students to write each step clearly and to justify their answers. Make sure that students understand that a proof must show a fact works in every case, not just for one example. Model to students how to structure their reasoning so it clearly shows a logical progression from the given information to the conclusion. Provide opportunities to spot errors in worked examples so they can recognise incomplete or incorrect reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not justify their answers or give reasons for why they have applied certain angle facts. • Students may write conclusions without clearly showing the logical steps that lead to them. • Students may assume that diagrams are drawn to scale when they are not. • Students may believe they have proven a fact when they have only shown it works for one case. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning from Year 8 on drawing and interpreting pie charts. Remind students that a pie chart represents a whole split into parts, with each sector showing a fraction of the total and all sectors summing to 360°. Make clear links between proportions, fractions and angles to show how they describe the same information. Emphasise the accurate use of a protractor when constructing sectors and highlight the importance of clear labelling. Introduce data given as percentages, fractions or bar charts for conversion into a pie chart. Encourage students to interpret pie charts by identifying key categories and, when comparing two charts, recognising that without totals only proportions can be compared. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may use the frequency as the angle size instead of working out the angle. • Students may not label the sectors. • When comparing two pie charts, students may assume equal sectors in different pie charts always represent the same frequency. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 7 learning on drawing and interpreting time series graphs. Remind them that these graphs show changes over time and require clearly labelled axes for accurate interpretation. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. Discuss with students how time series graphs with points joined by solid lines imply that it is possible to estimate information between data points, while points joined by dashed lines imply that the data between these points is not reliable. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may focus on specific points on a graph rather than the overall trends. • Students may assume that trends will always be consistent. • Students may use solid lines instead of dashed lines or vice versa. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 2 Mathematical talk • Does the time series graph have to start at zero? Explain your answer. • How can you show that your axis has not started from zero? • What does the overall trend of the graph show? • How can you describe the trend in this part of the graph? • Could there be a seasonal pattern? Explain your answer. • Is there a point that does not fit the general pattern? Why might that be? • Can the time series graph be used to estimate between data points? Explain your answer. • What similarities and what differences do you notice when comparing these two time series graphs? small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of cumulative frequency diagrams by interpreting the data shown. Remind students that each plotted point represents a cumulative total. Guide students to identify an estimate for the median and lower and upper quartiles by finding 25%, 50% and 75% of the total frequency and locating these values on the curve. Students then calculate the interquartile range by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile. They should also be able to compare two cumulative frequency diagrams by considering the median and interquartile range and deduce what these comparisons indicate. Encourage accurate reading of values by drawing horizontal and vertical lines and discuss why this method is more reliable than estimating by eye. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may attempt to find quartiles using the horizontal axis instead of the cumulative frequency axis. • Students may read values directly from the curve without drawing horizontal and vertical lines, resulting in inaccuracies. small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore parallel vectors, recognising that vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Students may have some understanding of this concept from earlier steps in this block. Highlight that parallel vectors have the same (or opposite) direction but may differ in magnitude. Support strategies for proving that column vectors are parallel by using vectors represented on grids to emphasise the link between vectors and scalars. After this, model how to prove that algebraic vectors are parallel through factorisation. Once students are confident, move on to more complex problems where they may need to consider vector journeys to compare two vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think vectors are parallel if they have the same magnitude. • Students may not recognise parallel vectors involving negative scalars. For example, writing 6 2 -   as –2 × -3 1   to show 6 2 -   and -3 1   are parallel. • Students may find it difficult to write algebraic expressions for vectors that represent movement in the opposite direction. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does it mean for two vectors to be parallel? • How can we tell if one column vector is a multiple of another? • Can two vectors be parallel but point in opposite directions? Explain how you know. • How can we tell if two vectors in terms of a and b are parallel? • What happens to a vector when it is multiplied by a negative scalar? • Why do parallel vectors not have to be equal in length? • Are two vectors that are equal in magnitude always parallel? small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and writing numbers as a product of prime factors from Key Stage 3. Use practical contexts to reinforce when HCF or LCM is needed, and model listing with small numbers to show why it becomes inefficient for greater values. Revisit prime factorisation using factor trees, emphasising that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation. Use Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that the HCF is the product of the common factors, while the LCM is the product of all factors within the diagram. Link back to listing to show both methods give the same result. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, particularly when using listing methods. • Students may rely on listing methods for large numbers, leading to inefficiency and increased likelihood of error. • Students may multiply all prime factors when finding the HCF, rather than only those common to all numbers. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 1 Mathematical talk • Explain what is meant by “highest common factor”. • Explain what is meant by “lowest common multiple”. • How can we decide whether a problem requires us to calculate the HCF or the LCM? • Can the HCF ever be greater than one of the numbers? Why or why not? • Is there more than one way to express 84 as a product of prime factors? • Does the order of the factors in a prime factorisation matter? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different between 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 23 × 3? • How do you find the HCF using a Venn diagram? • How do you find the LCM using a Venn diagram? small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by exploring how the number inside a square root affects how it can be simplified. Model how to simplify surds by rewriting the number inside the root as a product including a square factor, for example 18 = 9 × 2. Emphasise the importance of identifying a square factor as the result of square rooting a square number will be an integer. Highlight that it is often efficient to identify the greatest square factor to simplify a surd. If students cannot spot a square factor encourage the use of a factor tree to show the prime factorisation, for example 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 . Emphasise that this method relies on pairing equal factors to form a square number that can be square rooted. Once students are confident, extend this to other contexts such as area calculations or simplifying algebraic expressions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not fully simplify a surd, leaving a square factor inside the square root when more than one square factor is present. small_step_desc: In this small step, students rationalise denominators that contain a single surd, building on their understanding of surds and rational numbers. Model the process by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same surd so that the denominator becomes a rational number. For example, when the denominator is 2, multiply both the numerator and denominator by 2 so the denominator becomes 2. Emphasise that the value of the fraction does not change, only its form. Remind students to simplify the resulting fraction fully, including simplifying surds by considering square factors where possible. Keep the focus on single-term denominators such as 3 or 3 5. Rationalising denominators containing binomials will be covered later in the block. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may multiply only the denominator by the surd instead of multiplying both the numerator and denominator. • Students may think the value of the fraction changes when rationalising the denominator, rather than staying equivalent. • Students may not simplify fully after rationalising, including simplifying any surds or cancelling common factors. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 7 Mathematical talk • What does it mean for a denominator to be rational? • Why might it be useful to remove a surd from the denominator? • Does rationalising the denominator change the value of the fraction? Explain how you know. • How is rationalising the denominator similar to forming an equivalent fraction? • What is the product of a × a? • If the denominator is 2, what could we multiply by to make it rational? Why does this work? • Why must we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same value? • How do we know if a fraction is fully simplified? H National Curriculum links • Calculate exactly with fractions, {surds} and multiples of π; {simplify surd expressions involving squares [for example 12 = 4 × 3 = 4 × 3 = 2 3] and rationalise denominators}

small_step_desc: In this small step, students extend their understanding of expanding single brackets with surds to expanding and simplifying double brackets. Model expansion by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket, making all four products explicit. Area or grid models can help students see the structure and avoid missing terms. When simplifying after expansion, remind students that only like surds can be combined, and that surds may need further simplification by taking out square factors. This may lead to integer results or simpler surd forms. Once students are confident, they can be challenged with more complex expressions in the form (a + b c)(d + e c). Misconceptions and common errors • Students may only multiply the first and last terms in each brackets, for example writing ( 2 + 3)( 2 + 5) = 2 + 15 = 17 • Students may incorrectly simplify expressions, for example 10 + 5 2 + 2 + 2 = 19 • Students may not simplify products of surds where possible after expansion or may not realise it is possible for the final answer to be an integer. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about expanding (x + 2)(x + 5) and ( x + 2)( x + 5)? • When we multiply two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square root? Explain your answer. • Explain why 3 × 3 = 9 can be simplified, but 2 × 5 = 10 cannot be simplified further. • What do you notice when (a + b)(a – b) is expanded and simplified? Why do the surd terms cancel when simplifying? • What is the difference between simplifying a × a and simplifying a + a? • Can any of the surds in the resulting expansion be simplified further? Why or why not? small_step_name: Rationalise the denominator with more complex denominators (E)
small_step_desc: In this extend step, students will rationalise denominators with binomial expressions e.g. 1 + 5 2 Draw attention to the structure (a + b)(a – b), and highlight that this is a difference of two squares, simplifying to a2 – b, where the result will be an integer. Students will use this understanding to rationalise the denominator of a fraction, by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Emphasise that this is equivalent to multiplying by 1, so the value of the fraction does not change. Begin with examples such as 1 5 2 – where the denominator can be simplified to a positive integer, before moving on to more complex fractions such as 3 1 5 – where the denominator simplifies to a negative integer or 1 3 7 3 + + where the numerator has two terms. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may only multiply the denominator by the conjugate, changing the value of the fraction. • Students may multiply by the same denominator rather than the conjugate. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about 1 b and 1 + a b ? • If the denominator has two terms, how can we use the fact that (a + b)(a – b) æ a2 – b to remove the surd from the denominator? • Why must we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same expression? • How can we check that the value of the expression has not changed? • Why does the denominator simplify to an integer, or a rational number, in this method? • After rationalising the denominator, what further simplification might still be needed? small_step_desc: In this extend step, students develop their understanding of surds by expanding and simplifying single brackets involving surds. Begin with expanding single brackets and remind students that surds behave like algebraic terms and that the distributive law applies. Model expansion by multiplying each term inside the bracket by the term outside, using bar models or area models to support understanding. Once confident, students could be introduced to expanding and simplifying double brackets. Emphasise that only like surds can be combined. At this stage, avoid simplifying surds by factorising square factors, and instead focus on products that simplify directly to integers, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to combine unlike surds after expansion, for example trying to simplify 2 + 3 • Students may assume a × a = a rather than a. • Students may multiply the integer and the surd incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about expanding 3(x + 5) and 3( 2 + 5)? • What is the same and what is different about multiplying 3 × a and 3 × 5? • When we multiply two surds, what happens to the values inside the square root? • Explain why 2 × 2 = 4 can be simplified to an integer but 2 × 5 = 10 cannot. • Explain why 2 3 + 5 2 cannot be simplified. • What makes two surds “like surds”? Give an example. • Explain how you know when an expression with surds is fully simplified. F National Curriculum links • Simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions (including those involving surds) by: factorising quadratic expressions of the form x2 + bx + c, including the difference of two squares; simplifying expressions involving sums, products and powers, including the laws of indices E
